519.title: Before creation
519.hook: when no form was seen, no sin or virtue, no sun or moon, He alone was (Sukhmani 21)
519.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-first ashtpadi hear a series of when-questions about the time before creation, each answered by the One alone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sunn, the stillness, and your line: when there was nothing. Today the twenty-first ashtpadi asks a string of questions about that stillness.

Children are very good at one kind of question. Where was I before I was born? What was there before the house? Before the town? Before the world? Each answer moves the question back a step, until a parent says, gently, that's enough for tonight. The first stanza of Sukhmani's twenty-first ashtpadi asks those child's questions on purpose, one after another, and sends no one to bed. It walks them all the way back, to before creation.
screen: `WHERE WAS I BEFORE I WAS BORN?` → `BEFORE THE TOWN? BEFORE THE WORLD?` → `ALL THE WAY BACK.`

segments.voice: The stanza is built from questions, each beginning jab, when. In paraphrase: when there was no form to be seen, where would sin or virtue have come from? When He was absorbed in the stillness, against whom could anyone hold a grudge? When there was no color or mark, who could feel joy or sorrow? When there was only the Supreme, by Himself, who could be caught in attachment or doubt? Then the closing line: He set His own play in motion, and Nanak says, there is no other maker. Look at what the questions do. They take what fills an ordinary day, right and wrong, grudges, happiness, grief, worry, and quietly show that, in this picture, none of it is the floor. Before it, under it, there was the One. Yesterday's hymn in raag Maru fills in the sky for the same scene: no day or night, no moon or sun, only the One, in stillness. The word for form here is akaar: shape, outline, something you can see. Before creation there was no akaar at all. And notice what the stanza doesn't say. It doesn't call joys and sorrows fake. In its picture they belong to the play; they just aren't the deepest thing. There's a strange comfort in that. Whatever you're carrying this week, the grudge or the worry, there was a time before it, and Sukhmani says the One who was there then is here now.
screen: `JAB: A STRING OF WHEN QUESTIONS.` · `NO FORM, NO GRUDGE, NO SORROW.` · `AKAAR: NO SHAPE YET.` · `REAL, BUT NOT THE FLOOR.` · then, large: `HE ALONE WAS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let the room fade, the furniture, then the walls, the street, the city, the earth, the sun, like lights going out one at a time, and rest in the dark and the quiet before anything. Then slowly let things return, and notice what's still here. If you pray, rest in Waheguru in the stillness.
Before creation. Sukhmani asks: with no form yet, no grudge or sorrow, what was there? Its answer: the One alone, setting the play in motion.
Your line: he alone was. Before every worry, and under it, the One. See you tomorrow.

520.title: Creation begins
520.hook: by His will the play begins (Sukhmani 21)
520.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-first ashtpadi hear creation begin by God's hukam, as God's own play, after the stillness of sunn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, before creation, and your line: he alone was. Two days of stillness. Today, something moves.

A blank document, and a cursor blinking. Blink. Blink. Anyone who has had to write something knows that cursor. Everything you could say is still possible, and nothing has been said. Then you type the first word, and suddenly there's a direction, a voice, a shape. The page will never be blank in quite the same way again. After two days of stillness, the twenty-first ashtpadi reaches its first word.
screen: `THE CURSOR BLINKING.` → `THE FIRST WORD TYPED.` → `CREATION BEGINS.`

segments.voice: The stanzas of the twenty-first ashtpadi keep asking what was there before, and then, near the end, the scene changes. In paraphrase: when He Himself fashioned the world of forms, He spread it out through the three qualities; then sin and virtue came to be spoken of, some went to hell and some longed for heaven. Here's the shape of it. First the stillness, sunn. Then, by God's own choice, forms. Only then everything that fills our lives: right and wrong, reward and loss, hope and fear. They arrive with the world, not before it. The three qualities, the trigun, are an old Indian idea that Gurbani uses often: everything made is woven from three strands, roughly calm, restless and heavy. Gurbani treats them as part of the made world, which God stands beyond. What sets it all going? Sikh teaching answers with one word: hukam, God's will or order. In Japji, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: by His hukam forms are created; the hukam can't be described. And the picture Sukhmani keeps returning to is a play, khel. God sets His own khel in motion, and is in it. That word matters. A play isn't a machine, ground out because it must be. It's made freely, with delight. Sikh teaching doesn't say why God began the play, beyond that it was God's will. It leaves the why with the One who began it.

segments.voice: Sit for a moment in stillness, the way the ashtpadi did. Then make one tiny beginning right where you are, the first sentence of a letter, one line in a notebook, the first step of a recipe, and notice the shift from nothing to something, without needing to know the ending. If you pray, begin with Waheguru.
Khel, play or game: by God's hukam the stillness gives way to forms, and the world, with all its right and wrong, starts as God's own khel.
Your line: the play begins. Made freely, the way a play is. Day five hundred twenty, done.

521.title: Living ashtpadi 21
521.hook: the vast and the quiet behind all things
521.tomorrow: Ashtpadi 22, salok: Lord of all beings
521.howItsDone: Sikh practice values rising at amrit vela, the hours before dawn that Japji names as the time to reflect on the Name, for quiet remembrance before the day begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, khel, and your line: the play begins. Today the stillness and the beginning step out into an ordinary morning.

Right before dawn, the sky does something odd. It isn't dark and it isn't light. It goes a deep, even gray-blue, and everything is very quiet: no birds yet, no traffic, the trees just shapes. Then color comes in from one edge, a line of pale yellow, then pink, and all at once it's morning, and the noise of the day begins. In a small way, the twenty-first ashtpadi plays out every dawn.
screen: `THE GRAY-BLUE BEFORE DAWN.` → `A LINE OF PALE YELLOW.` → `EVERY DAWN, THE ASHTPADI.`

segments.voice: Here's the twenty-first ashtpadi in brief. Before anything, the Formless One, nirankaar, rested in sunn, the deep stillness: no form, no grudge, no joy or sorrow, only the One. Then, by God's own will, the play began, and the world of forms spread out. Living that doesn't mean thinking about the beginning of the universe all day. It means remembering that the stillness didn't go anywhere. In Sikh teaching, the One who rested in sunn is the same One inside the play now, behind all things, the way the quiet gray sky is still there behind the sunrise. That's one reason Sikh practice values amrit vela, the hours before dawn. In Japji, Guru Nanak names that ambrosial hour as the time to reflect on the greatness of the Name. It's the time of day that looks most like the ashtpadi: quiet first, then the world. Sitting with the Name then is a way to meet the stillness before the noise begins, and carry a little of it into the noise. And the noise is not the enemy. Sikh teaching has no quarrel with the busy day; the Gurus worked, farmed, traded and led. The point is that behind the busyness there's something vast and quiet the busyness can't touch. Some mornings it's easy to sense, and some mornings it isn't. Sukhmani says it's there either way.
screen: `STILLNESS, THEN THE PLAY.` · `THE STILLNESS DIDN'T GO ANYWHERE.` · `AMRIT VELA: QUIET FIRST.` · `THE BUSY DAY IS NOT THE ENEMY.` · then, large: `BEHIND ALL THINGS.`

segments.voice: Look at whatever sky is outside your window now, or, if you can't, remember a dawn you've seen, and let your breath be as slow as the sky changing. Notice the quiet underneath the color, or underneath the light and noise of the day. If you pray, rest in Waheguru, behind all things.
Nirankaar, the Formless One: the stillness nirankaar rested in before creation is still here, behind the play; amrit vela, before dawn, is a daily way to meet it.
Your line: behind all things. Quiet first, then the world, and the quiet stays. Until tomorrow.

522.title: Ashtpadi 22, salok: Lord of all beings
522.hook: jeea jant ke thaakuraa: Lord of all beings, pervading all (Sukhmani 22)
522.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-second ashtpadi begin with a salok naming God the Master of all living beings, the One spread through every creature.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nirankaar, and your line: behind all things. The twenty-first ashtpadi brought the world into being; the twenty-second looks at who lives in it.

A single ant on the kitchen counter, walking a careful line toward a grain of sugar. The usual reflex is a paper towel, or a thumb. But stop and actually watch it, and it's remarkable. It's carrying something heavier than itself. It's checking the way with its antennae. It's going somewhere, for some reason that matters to it. The twenty-second ashtpadi of Sukhmani opens by naming the Lord of that ant, and of everything else that breathes.
screen: `ONE ANT ON THE COUNTER.` → `IT'S GOING SOMEWHERE.` → `THE LORD OF EVERYTHING THAT BREATHES.`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: Lord and Master of all beings and creatures, You Yourself are present in all of them. Nanak says: the One is spread out everywhere; where could a second be seen? Start with jeea jant. Jeea are living beings, things with life and breath. Jant are creatures, every kind of animal. Together it's Gurbani's way of saying everyone and everything alive: people, ants, birds, fish, the cat on the windowsill. Thaakur is lord or master, a word of respect for the one in charge. So the salok begins: Master of every living thing. But the second half changes what master means. God isn't pictured as a landlord far off, collecting rent. Aape vartanhaar: God Himself is the one moving within them all, present and active in each. Then the last line: eko pasariaa. The One has spread out. Where is there a second to see? This is one root of the respect Sikh teaching shows to living things. If the same One is spread through every creature, the ant on the counter isn't simply a pest or a stranger. In the salok's picture, it's kin: made by the same Master, filled by the same presence. This isn't a rule about every mosquito. It means the glance you give a living thing can carry a little respect. The ashtpadi begins by widening the circle of who counts.

segments.voice: Find a living thing you can see or hear, a bird outside, a houseplant, a pet, a fly on the window, even a picture of an animal you love, and watch its breathing, its movement, the way it pays attention to its world. Then hold the thought quietly: the same Master, the same life. If you pray, rest in Waheguru as you watch.
Thaakur, lord or master: its salok calls God thaakur of jeea jant, Master of every living thing, and says the One is spread through them all.

523.title: In every heart
523.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-second ashtpadi hear that God dwells ghat ghat, in every heart, a teaching lived out in langar's shared rows and in seva to all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, thaakur, and your line: lord of all. The circle widened to every living thing; today it moves inward, to the heart.

A subway car at rush hour. Forty strangers, shoulder to shoulder, all carefully not looking at one another. A man in a suit reading his phone. A teenager with headphones and eyes closed. A grandmother with grocery bags, a nurse just off a night shift. Each face closed, like a house with the curtains drawn. You could ride with them every day for a year and never know one name. The twenty-second ashtpadi makes a claim about every one of those closed houses: someone lives inside.
screen: `FORTY STRANGERS, NOT LOOKING.` → `EACH FACE A CLOSED HOUSE.` → `SOMEONE LIVES INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's salok said the One is spread through all beings. The twenty-second ashtpadi presses the point home: God dwells in every heart, ghat ghat, in each body and each being. Ghat literally means a pot or vessel, a clay jar. Gurbani uses it for the body, and for the heart inside it, the way a jar holds water. Doubled, ghat ghat means in every single one. Gurbani returns to this again and again. In Sohila, the prayer before sleep, Guru Nanak sings, in paraphrase: within all is the Light, and You are that Light; by its shining, everything shines. Every face on that subway car is a clay jar with the same Light inside. This is the ground under some very practical things Sikhs do. It's why the langar, the free kitchen, seats everyone on the floor in the same rows, whoever they are. It's why the Gurus spoke so sharply against treating people as high or low by caste. And it's why, for Sikhs, seva, serving others, is never only charity: if the Light is in every heart, serving a stranger is serving the One who lives there. It's a demanding teaching. It's easy to see the Light in a smiling child or a kind friend, and harder in the man who shoved past you for a seat. Sukhmani makes no exception for him. Ghat ghat means every jar.
screen: `GHAT GHAT: IN EVERY VESSEL.` · `THE SAME LIGHT IN EACH.` · `THE GROUND UNDER LANGAR AND SEVA.` · `NO EXCEPTIONS, EVEN THE RUDE ONE.` · then, large: `EVERY HEART.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ordinary face, not your favorite person in the world, or look at one nearby or in a photo, and take in the eyes, the lines, the expression. Hold the thought, there's Light in this jar too, and if that comes easily, try a harder face. If you pray, say Waheguru softly as you look.
Ghat ghat, in every vessel: Sukhmani says God dwells in every vessel, every body and heart, and Sohila adds that the same Light shines in all.
Your line: every heart. Each face on the train, the same Light inside. Same time tomorrow.

524.title: Sustainer of all
524.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib hear that God sustains every creature, and each evening in Rehras recite Guru Arjan's hymn picturing food set out even for creatures within rocks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghat ghat, and your line: every heart. The Master of all beings, found inside each one; today, who feeds them.

Split a rock in a field, and sometimes there's a tiny creature living inside: a beetle in a damp hollow, a grub, a pale little worm. Nobody brings it groceries. Nobody checks on it. And yet there it is, alive, with what it needs. Guru Arjan, the same Guru who wrote Sukhmani, used exactly that picture in a hymn Sikhs recite every evening, and it's the picture under today's line from the twenty-second ashtpadi.
screen: `A CREATURE INSIDE A ROCK.` → `NOBODY BRINGS IT GROCERIES.` → `THE SUSTAINER OF ALL.`

segments.voice: The twenty-second ashtpadi, which began by naming God the Master of all beings, says that God sustains each one of them. The word Sikhs often use for that sustenance is rijak: daily bread, livelihood, what keeps a creature alive. Guru Arjan unfolds the idea in a hymn in raag Gujri that's part of Rehras, the evening prayer. In paraphrase: why, mind, do you scheme and worry, when God Himself is busy caring for you? Even in rocks and stones He made creatures, and set their food before them. Then a second picture. A migrating crane flies hundreds of kos, the old measure of distance, leaving her young behind. Who feeds them? Who teaches them to eat? Have you never thought of that? The chicks alone, the mother far away, and still they're fed. Now, what this teaching isn't. It isn't a promise that no one will ever go hungry, and it isn't permission to stop working. Sikhs are taught kirat karni, honest work, and langar feeds whoever comes, because people do go hungry; Sikhs see feeding them as God's work done through human hands. The point is about worry. Guru Arjan isn't telling the mind to stop trying. He's telling it to stop scheming and fretting as if everything depended on it alone. And often, Sikhs would say, the way God feeds someone is through you.
screen: `RIJAK: WHAT KEEPS A CREATURE ALIVE.` · `IN ROCKS AND STONES, FOOD SET OUT.` · `THE CRANE FLIES; THE CHICKS ARE FED.` · `NOT A REASON TO STOP WORKING.` · then, large: `HE FEEDS ALL.`

segments.voice: If you have a pet, give it a little food or fresh water now, slowly; if not, put a few crumbs on a windowsill or water a plant, then sit and breathe. Watch, or picture, the creature receiving it, and notice that for this moment you're part of how it's sustained. If you pray, say Waheguru as you give.
Rijak, sustenance or livelihood: Sukhmani says God sustains each creature with its rijak; Guru Arjan pictures food set out even in rocks, and a crane's chicks fed while she's far away.
Your line: he feeds all. The worry can loosen its grip. Day five hundred twenty-four counts.

525.title: Living ashtpadi 22
525.tomorrow: Ashtpadi 23, salok: the ointment of wisdom
525.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-second ashtpadi hear that every living being belongs to the One, and Sikh tradition remembers Guru Har Rai for his care of gardens, animals and the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rijak, and your line: he feeds all. A week ends today: before creation, the play beginning, the quiet behind all things, the Lord of all, every heart, and the One who feeds every creature.

Sikhs tell a story about the seventh Guru, Guru Har Rai, when he was a boy. Walking through a garden in a long, flowing robe, he brushed past a flowering bush, and a few petals fell to the ground. His grandfather, Guru Hargobind, saw it and told him gently that a robe that wide must be carried with care. The boy, the story goes, was so moved that he kept that care all his life.
screen: `A BOY, A ROBE, A FLOWERING BUSH.` → `A FEW PETALS FALL.` → `CARRY IT WITH CARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the twenty-second ashtpadi in brief. God is the thaakur, the Master, of jeea jant, every living being. The One is spread through them all, dwelling ghat ghat, in every heart, and sustaining each creature with its daily bread. Put together, one plain line: everything alive is His. Living it starts with how we touch things. The story of Guru Har Rai is passed down in Sikh tradition rather than recorded in the Guru Granth Sahib, but its point fits the ashtpadi exactly. If every living thing belongs to the One, a flower isn't just scenery and an animal isn't just a resource. They're in someone else's care, and we're walking through the garden. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Har Rai as a lover of gardens and animals, and as someone who kept medicines to give to the sick, including, by many accounts, the son of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, whose family were no friends of the Gurus. That detail matters. Everything alive is His, including the people we'd rather not help. In practice, this can be very small: watering the office plant everyone forgets, driving a little slower past the park, asking how the elderly neighbor's dog is doing. None of it is grand. But each small act says: this life isn't mine to waste. It belongs to the One who is spread through all.
screen: `THE ASHTPADI: MASTER, PRESENT, FEEDER.` · `A STORY PEOPLE TELL.` · `MEDICINE FOR AN ENEMY'S SON.` · `SMALL ACTS OF CARE.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING ALIVE IS HIS.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was food; today is care. Tend one living thing slowly, a plant that needs water, litter on the path outside, a tired person at home who'd like a cup of tea, as if it belonged to someone you love, because in the ashtpadi's picture it does; or, if nothing is nearby, picture the one you'll care for later. If you pray, say Waheguru as you tend it.
Jeea, living beings, those with life and breath: every jeea has the same Master, the same indwelling Light, the same Feeder; so every living thing is handled with care.
Your line: everything alive is his. Seven days, from the stillness to the garden. See you tomorrow.
